The build is fine, but I would definitely save your spare change and get an entry level GPU on down the line. A $150 GTX 1050 or AMD equivalent will be roughly thrice as powerful as your 7750. That's the difference between fiddling with settings all the time and not having to worry about it.
Tip: the more money you spend now, the more money you will save in the future. Buying old parts (although cheap) will just cost you in the long run.

ABOUT THE CASE - scrape up some extra money and maybe go for the good noise suppression case - I did and don't regret it at all - the computer is nearly silent.

Also - FANS - you need a lot more fans than before - especially a top of the line cpu fan - Triple Check your build to see that everything will fit inside the case with the fans installed, and that there is adequate enough power, and power connectors, to run the whole show.

This is all a lot more important today than it was back in 2000, and it is super easy to fuck it up. You are better to find the extra $200 and buy the better gear in regards to case, cpu cooler, and case fans. Gotta keep it cool and the new PC's are very hot. They run a lot more power under the hood.

For example, I am running a double CPU fan - side ejected, another internal fan on the video chip, and six case fans, (two on the back, one on the top, two on the front, one internal across the ram and mainboard,) in addition to the power supply fan. Under load it can still get too warm for my liking. The noise factor is also real, hence the suppression case.

Double check to be sure your PSU has the adequate connectors you will need, including the internal cord length to reach everything.

Also the wall circuit - the new PC's pull a lot more current - I had to rearrange the usage on the circuit after tripping the breaker a couple of times running a heater on the same circuit as the new PC. Never an issue with the old PC.

Avoid ASRock boards. Their platform support for Ryzen has been pretty poor (im running an ASRock X370 now). Asus seems to have the best support and platform stability right now.

You should also consider saving a few more bucks to go for 16GB of RAM instead of 8. More and more PC games have a minimum requirement of 8GB RAM. Having that extra RAM will make your PC more future proof in general. Also double check the timings of your RAM, since RAM speeds actually matter with Ryzen. Im running 3200 @ CL14 (stock XMP for my sticks), which in my case is faster than overclocking 3600 @ CL16.

Also going to agree with the other guys in saying to go for the SATA SSD instead of the M.2. Windows will still be booting in under 10 sec with the SATA drive.

If you're installing Window's, create an official installation disk for free from the Microsoft Website. Install windows and update drivers and everything as necessary.

At this point, you'll have windows installed, but not "activated" with a product key. Websearch for "Windows Loader 2.2.2," then download, install, and run it. This program searches for a product key that will work, then activates it. As far as Microsoft is concerned, it's a legitimate version of windows (because it technically is, you just didn't pay for the product key).

P.S. Your antivirus will probably try to block Windows Loader.
